The Past Perfect vs. The Simple Past

You use the Past Perfect to report what people said. When people say something using either the Present Perfect or Simple Past, you need to change those tense to the Past Perfect when you report they have said or asked.
Refer to the chart for an outline of how these tense change to the Past Perfect in reported speech.

Perfect Infinitives vs. Infinitives
You know the infinitive as to + verb. You can sometimes use an infinitive without the to (bare infinitive). It depends on what verb precedes the infinitive.

Infinitives themselves do not change in meaning whether they are used in an active or passive way, or if they are used in different tenses. What is important is what verb you use them with - this will affect the tense of the infinitive.
Compare these two types of infinitives in their active and passive forms:

The Simple Infinitive refers to the same time as the verb which precedes it.

For example:
I was happy to meet her.
My daughter's teacher is said to be very strict.
The Perfect Infinitive refers to a time period before the preceding verb refers to.

For example:
I'm glad to have met her.
John was thought to have left earlier.

images.text:
Back in '33, Grandad was just a child in school. To tell you the truth, he was actually quite lucky, because his parents were fortunate to still have some money. They didn't have enough money to have been rich by any means, but in those days, it wasn't unheard of to have lost your entire life's savings.
People found that banks had gone broke by the dozen. In the evenings the grown-ups talked about families they said had lost their homes that day. The banks, they thought, were to blame for everybody's unhappiness.

One spring morning after he brought in the paper, they found that yet another bank had been robbed, and in plain daylight! Grandad would soon come to know the bank robber well. John Herbert Dillinger was his name. He and his friends found that reading about the robberies helped them pass the time. He admitted that from the start they had devoured every story that was published about Dillinger and his gang.
His parents said that the way he had eagerly awaited the morning paper to see if perhaps another robbery had been committed, was shameful. Grandad followed Dillinger's movements on a map and was known to have cheered him on each time he dodged the law. They had made lists of the hotels where he stayed, and of the police officers who had lamented their unlucky misses.

The most exciting Dillinger exploit was the Bohemia blunder. Dillinger and the gang, needing rest and relaxation, turned up at the Little Bohemia Lodge. The owners were glad to have gotten the business, but terrified to have discovered who their guests actually were.
The papers reported that lady of the house had snuck out a letter alerting the FBI. Agents assembled and surrounded the buildings! Then, they heard dogs barking. By the time they got into the building, they discovered that Dillinger had escaped with five of his gang members.
When Grandad and his friends read the account of Bohemia blunder, they all breathed a sigh of relief. Dillinger had outwitted the authorities once again. The adventure was to continue!
